title: When To Reteach A Routine
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that routines break down not because students are individually defiant but because a teacher failed to teach them with enough detail the first time, and he lays out when and how to reteach one. He distinguishes between everyday enforcement (holding individuals accountable through the classroom management plan) and the rarer moment when most of the class is off-track at once, which signals a teaching failure rather than a discipline problem. His central move is treating a sloppy routine as the teacher's responsibility to fix through re-teaching in greater detail, modeling what not to do, and raising the performance bar, rather than through consequences aimed at individual students. He also stresses close, constant observation while routines are performed so that reminders come before misbehavior rather than after.
points: Reteach a routine only when most of the class is off-track at the same time, not when one or two students misbehave individually.
If a routine unravels mid-transition, send the class back to repeat it immediately when possible, or reteach later once you have class time.
Reminders given before misbehavior are always good; reminders given after misbehavior are always bad and should be replaced by following the plan.
Reteaching should include modeling in greater detail, showing what not to do, and raising your stated performance expectations.
quotes: So when should you reteach a routine? When most of your students are off-track at the same time and thus you’re unable to hold them individually accountable.
It bears mentioning that the second you notice your class going off the rails, it’s best to send them back to their seats or the previous transition to repeat the routine.
An overall sloppy or bad routine, however, is on you because it proves there is something your class isn’t understanding.
Regardless of what it is, the way to correct it is to reteach the routine in greater detail. It doesn’t matter the grade level.
To have a well-behaved and high-achieving class in this day and age you must establish and maintain a culture of excellence that pervades every moment of the school day.
